extracted.intended_audience: scientists, naturalists, and philosophers concerned with scientific language, taxonomy, and method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for constructing precise scientific language (terminology and nomenclature) and for forming natural classifications that best aid induction, memory, and the discovery of laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact descriptive terminology for observable phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Language should allow exact description of impressions on outward senses and inward feelings that are uniformly connected with outward objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjective sensations (e.g., from disease) resist exact naming because others cannot verify identity of experience. In sciences dealing with external objects (botany, mineralogy) descriptive terminology can be carried to high perfection; examples include the detailed botanical terms for leaf division and mineral descriptors like lustre and crystalline form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixation and consistency of term meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms should be fixed so the same word is always used in the same sense and the same idea is always expressed by the same words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tournefort first perceived utility; Linnaeus 'created and fixed' botanical language. Fixed terminology sheds clearness and precision over a science by enabling reliable communication and recognition of concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise names for frequently used abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequently recurring abstract conceptions obtained by comparison should be given brief, compact names to concentrate attention and aid thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short names (e.g., 'limit,' 'momentum,' 'delegation' vs 'representation') save cognitive load, fix ideas in memory, and facilitate discovery and communication of complex relations that would otherwise require long paraphrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of nomenclature: name every Kind (infima species)
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a name for every Kind (lowest Kind or infima species) encountered in a branch of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good systematic examples: Linnaean biological nomenclature and chemical nomenclature (Lavoisier, Guyton-Morveau). When new lowest Kinds are discovered, names should be assigned according to a uniform principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature terms must connote both properties and Kind-status
rubrics_metrics.description: A nomenclature-word connotes certain attributes and also connotes that those attributes are distinctive of a Kind (i.e., the word's form signals it names an infima species).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although such names denote a Kind, their meaning can be unfolded by a definition (set of characters). The definition plus the form of the word together constitute the full meaning; definitions may be revised without necessarily altering the functional use of the name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions in nomenclature should function as real discriminators
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of characters used to discriminate each Kind should constitute a true definition enabling recognition and application of the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If definitions prove insufficient to pick out a single Kind (i.e., several Kinds are confounded), the application of the name must be revised; the connotation (the diagnostic characters) guides application and is therefore the meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Throw meaning into word-formation to avoid mechanical use
rubrics_metrics.description: Words should be formed so that their derivation and analogy keep alive the consciousness of what they signify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Languages that form compounds and derivatives from native roots (e.g., German, Greek) have advantages. Morphological transparency helps prevent words from degenerating into empty counters used without sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent mechanical (meaningless) use of language where reasoning is non-mechanical
rubrics_metrics.description: When reasoning cannot safely be carried on mechanically, language should be constructed to make merely mechanical use difficult or impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic symbols are appropriate where operations can be mechanical (arithmetic, parts of geometry reduced to numbers). But for most sciences, using symbols as counters (without imagery) undermines the need to keep phenomena concretely in mind; language should instead force continual attention to meaning and particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve symbol-like mechanical language for truly mechanical processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolic, counter-like notation (as in algebra) is ideal only where the subject permits reasoning to be performed mechanically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebra's perfection lies in enabling manipulation without thinking of referents. Outside numeric reasoning, many deductive steps require keeping the real phenomena and their peculiarities constantly in mind; thus unmeaning symbols are generally unsuitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain continual acquaintance with concrete phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists must continually 'stamp' meaning into terms by habitual contemplation of the real phenomena, not by living among formulae alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one relies only on formulas and stops engaging with the realities from which laws were derived, one will misapply formulas, lose their meaning, and cease to recognize when cases fall under a formula's applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification should order ideas to best promote memory and discovery of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of classification is to group things and arrange groups so as to best conduce to remembrance and to the ascertainment of their laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification as an act of the mind is a contrivance for ordering ideas to give greatest command over existing knowledge and to lead most directly to acquiring more; it should concern real objects and embrace all really existing objects relevant to the domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer properties that are causes or sure marks of many other properties when classifying
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification properties should, if possible, be those that are causes of many other properties or sure indications of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes are preferable because they are most direct and useful; where cause cannot be used diagnostically, select prominent effects of the cause that reliably mark other properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor Natural (scientific) over Artificial (technical) classification
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific or natural classification groups objects so that many important general propositions can be asserted about the group, unlike artificial systems based on arbitrarily selected circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural classification places together objects similar in general aspect and yields many and important common properties; artificial classifications (e.g., grouping by a single trivial property) can be mischievous by habituating thought in unhelpful groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the whole of nature when constituting classes
rubrics_metrics.description: To properly constitute any one class, one must determine its place in a general division of the whole of nature and consider all objects with any affinity to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic arrangements (e.g., of plants, animals) require that families and larger classes be formed with reference to the general division of the whole domain; isolated family-level decisions are inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing classification on merely simple, easily perceived properties if they lack usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting properties for classification simply because they are simple or perceptible at first sight may not serve the ends of scientific classification if those properties do not lead to important common propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tournefort's corolla-shape and the Linnaean stamen/pistil counts are easy to apply but often fail to produce groups with many useful common predicates; such arrangements can mislead habitual thought and impede scientific ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standardized numerical scales for properties where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, express certain properties by numerical or classified scales to provide precision and comparability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Werner's color scale in mineralogy and Mohs' numerical hardness scale; some properties (specific gravity) give numerical measures directly, while others (crystalline form) may require mathematical analysis to quantify relations and gradations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish terminology from nomenclature and apply each appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminology comprises descriptive terms for attributes; nomenclature is the system of names for Kinds—both are essential but distinct components of a philosophical language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms like those of Lavoisier are nomenclatural. Terminology covers words like 'linear', 'serrated'; nomenclature covers binomial names like 'Viola odorata'. The two elements serve different roles and should be constructed with their purposes in mind.
